- 20.1 Magnets and Magnetic Fields Magnets and Magnetic poles -Magnet: An object surrounded by a magnetic field and has the property of attracting ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt).
- ◼ A compass needle is simply a bar magnet which is supported at its center of gravity so that it can rotate freely.
- Magnetic poles: the area of a magnet where the magnetic effect is stronges -Every magnet is polarized.
- Every magnet has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S).
- N pole is the north -seeking pole, and S pole is the south -seeking pole.
- ◼ Between m agnets, Like Poles Repel; Unlike Poles Attract.
- Magnetic poles always appear in pairs.
- Monopoles of magnet do not exist.
- Magnetism and Magnetic domain -Ferromagnetism: Iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, and some of their oxides and alloys, show strong magnetic effects.
- Source of ferromagnetism: ◼ The spinning and orbiting motion of the electrons make each atom a tiny magnet.
- ◼ A cluster of billions of atoms that all have magnetic fields that are lines up in the same way.
- So they form a magnetic domain.
- Each domain is like a tiny magnet.
- ◼ Magneti zation:  An unmagnetized piece of iron is made up of domains that are randomly arranged.
-  In a magnet, the domains are aligned in one direction (down), and may be altered in size by the magnetization process.
- Induced Magnetism: ◼ Both N/S magnetic poles attract metal such as iron, steel.
- ◼ Unmagnetized materials such as steel and iron acquire two opposite magnetic poles when placed in neighborhood of a magnet.
- That is how magnetism is induced.
- Making a magnet ◼ Place the unmagnetized material near a magnet.
- This gains weak magnetism.
- ◼ Electromagnet: Make direct current passing through a coil of wire placed outside the materials.
- Hard and Soft magnetic materials: Depending on how well they keep their magnetism ◼ Hard magnetic materials  Difficult to magnetized but do not readily lose their magnetism.
-  Used for permanent magnets Examples: Steel, and alloys called Alnico, Alcomax and Magnadur ◼ Soft magnetic materials  Relatively easy t magnetize, but their magnetism is only temporary.
-  Used for temporary magnets.
- They are used in the cores of electromagnets and transformers, because their magnetic effect can be “switched ” on or off or reversed easily.
- Examples: Iron(soft iron) and Mumetal -Non -magnetic materials: Include metals such as brass, copper, zinc, tin, and aluminum, as well as non -metals.
- Demagnetize a magnet  Drop a magnet on the floor or strike it with a hammer.
- The principle is to jar the domains into randomness and the magnet loses some or all of its magnetism.
-  Heating a permanent magnet.
- The principle is that raising the temperature increases the random thermal motion of atoms, which tends to randomize the domains.
- Above a certain temperature, it loses the property of ferromagnetism.

- Earth as a magnet-Earth ’s magnetism is due to the circulation of the molten metal within Earth ’s core ◼ The earth is a large weak magnet with the magnetic S -seeking pole under a point in Canada.
- Magnetic Declination: The angular difference between the direction of a compass needle (which points along the magnetic field lines) at any location and true (geographical) north.
- The angle of dip or The angle of inclination: The angle that the Earth’s magnetic field makes with the horizontal at any point.
- The Earth’s magnetic field at most locations is not tangent to the Earth’s surface.
- Magnetic poles reverse themselves periodically.
- Earth’s north magnetic pole has been moving over time, on the order of 10 km per year in recent decades.
- Magnetism in rocks solidified at various times in the past (age determined by radioactive dating) suggested that poles reversed direction 400 times over the last 330 million years.

- Magnetic field around a wire: If an electric current is passed through a wire, a weak magnetic field is produced.
- The magnetic field has these features: ◼ the magnetic field lines are circles ◼ the field is strongest close to the wire ◼ increasing the current increases the strength of the field.
- Direction of the current (I) determines the direction of the magnetic field (B).

# 18.1 The Electric Battery

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Galvani, Volta and the argument that produced the battery

In the 1780s **Luigi Galvani** carried out a series of experiments on the contraction of a frog's leg muscles using electricity produced by static electricity. He concluded that the source of the electric charge lay in the frog's muscle or nerve itself, and that the metal merely transmitted the charge to the proper points. He named this charge *animal electricity*.

**Alessandro Volta** disagreed. He believed the source of the electricity was the contact between the two dissimilar metals — that is, a chemical reaction of oxidation and reduction — rather than anything in the animal.

To test this he placed a piece of cloth soaked in salt solution or dilute acid between a disc of zinc and one of silver, and piled up a "battery" of such couplings. When strips of metal connected to the two ends of the pile were brought close together, a spark was produced. On this basis he designed and built the first electric battery; he published the discovery in 1800. The guide prints 1900 here; that is an error — Volta's pile dates to 1800, immediately after Galvani's experiments of the 1780s.

The word *battery* still carries Volta's meaning: a pile of separate couplings acting together.

## Cells and batteries

A **battery** produces electricity by transforming chemical energy into electrical energy. It is made of several electric cells connected together.

An electric cell has three parts:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Electrodes** | Two plates or rods made of dissimilar metals. The positive $(+)$ electrode is the **cathode** — for example carbon, copper or silver. The negative $(-)$ electrode is the **anode** — for example zinc or aluminium. |
| **Electrolyte** | The solution the electrodes are immersed in (wet batteries), or a paste (dry batteries). Sulfuric acid is a wet example. |
| **Terminal** | The part of each electrode that lies outside the solution. |

Dry cells are the ones normally used, because wet cells are easy to spill or leak, which is neither safe nor convenient.

## How an electric cell works

Take sulfuric acid as the electrolyte, zinc as the anode and copper as the cathode.

**1. The acid dissolves the anode.**

$$\mathrm{H_2SO_4 \rightarrow 2H^+ + SO_4^{2-}} \qquad \mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

**2. Two electrons stay behind, making the anode negative.** The positive $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ ion enters the sulfuric acid and makes the acid positive:

$$\mathrm{Zn^{2+} + SO_4^{2-} \rightarrow ZnSO_4}$$

so the acid is now $\mathrm{ZnSO_4}$ together with $\mathrm{2H^+}$.

**3. Electrons are pulled off the copper cathode.**

$$\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

**4. The positive $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ion stays behind, making the cathode positive.** The two electrons enter the acid and make it neutral again:

$$\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow 2H}$$

The opposite charges now sitting on the two electrodes create a potential difference, and so chemical energy is made available as electrical energy.

(The guide names the electrode in step 3 as the carbon cathode, but the example it sets up uses copper and its own equation is written for $\mathrm{Cu}$; read it as the copper cathode.)

## Why a disconnected cell does not run down

Whether the cell keeps reacting depends entirely on whether the terminals are joined:

- **Terminals not connected.** Only a small amount of zinc dissolves. As the zinc anode becomes increasingly negative, new positive zinc ions produced at it are attracted straight back to the anode, so the reaction stalls and a voltage is simply maintained.
- **Terminals connected.** Charge is now allowed to flow between the terminals, so far more zinc can dissolve. One electrode is used up after a time and the cell goes "dead".

This is why an unconnected cell simply holds its voltage, while a cell left joined into a circuit is eventually used up.

## What sets the voltage

The voltage a cell produces depends on the material of the electrodes and on their relative ability to be dissolved or to give up electrons.

It does **not** depend on the size of the cell. Smaller cells contain fewer reactants and therefore produce less electrical energy in total, but the voltage does not change.

## Cells in series

When two or more cells are connected with the positive terminal of one joined to the negative terminal of the next, they are connected **in series**, and their voltages add:

$$\mathrm{EMF_{battery}} = n(\text{cells}) \times \mathrm{EMF_{cell}}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Battery** | A device that produces electricity by transforming chemical energy into electrical energy; several electric cells connected together |
| **Electrodes** | Plates or rods made of dissimilar metals, one positive and one negative, immersed in the electrolyte |
| **Cathode** | The positive $(+)$ electrode, e.g. carbon, copper, silver |
| **Anode** | The negative $(-)$ electrode, e.g. zinc, aluminium |
| **Electrolyte** | The solution (wet batteries) or paste (dry batteries) in which the electrodes are immersed |
| **Terminal** | The part of each electrode outside the solution |
| **Connected in series (cells)** | Positive terminal of one cell joined to the negative terminal of another, so that the voltages add |

# 18.2 Electric Current

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The circuit

An **electric circuit** is a continuous conducting path connected between the terminals of a battery — so there is a potential difference across it. Its elements are the battery, a device run by electrical energy (the resistance), conducting wires, and a switch.

Three kinds of circuit are distinguished:

| Circuit | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Complete circuit** | A continuous conducting path |
| **Open circuit** | There is a break in the circuit, so no current flows |
| **Short circuit** | Two wires that should not have touched have touched, so the current is shortened |

In many real circuits the wires are connected to a common conductor, called the **ground**, to provide continuity.

## What a current is

The purpose of a battery is to produce a potential difference, and a potential difference is what makes charges move. Potential difference is the same thing as voltage, so voltage provides the force that pushes charge through a circuit. When a complete circuit is formed, any flow of charge through the wires is called an electric current.

**Electric current** is the net amount of charge that passes through the wire's full cross-section at any point, per unit time:

$$I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$$

where $I$ is the electric current in amperes (A), $\Delta Q$ is the amount of charge that passes through in coulombs (C), and $\Delta t$ is the time interval in seconds (s).

The unit is the **ampere (A)**, named after André Ampère:

$$1\ \mathrm{A} = 1\ \mathrm{C/s} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{mA} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A} \qquad 1\ \mu\mathrm{A} = 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{A}$$

Current is a **scalar**. Its direction along a given wire is constant, but it is not a vector quantity.

## Conventional current and electron current

Two directions have to be kept apart:

- **Conventional current** is the direction in which positive charge would flow: from high potential to low potential. This convention was fixed before the electron was discovered, and it is still the one used today.
- **Electron current** is the direction electrons actually flow: from low potential to high potential.

Nothing is lost by keeping the old convention, because positive charges flowing in one direction is exactly equivalent to negative charges flowing in the opposite direction.

## Conservation of electric charge

Charge does not disappear. A steady current is, at any instant, the same at one point of the circuit as at any other point. A battery does not create or destroy charge, and a lightbulb does not destroy or create charge either — the battery supplies the potential difference and the bulb converts energy, but the quantity of charge passing per second is the same all the way round.

## Measuring current

An **ammeter** is a device that measures electric current. Because the whole current must pass through it, it is connected **in series**. Its own resistance $R_{\text{ammeter}} \approx 0$, so it can be treated as a piece of wire and does not change the circuit it is measuring.

Its measurement ranges are $0$–$3\ \mathrm{A}$ and $0$–$0.6\ \mathrm{A}$. Use the larger range first to prevent damage to the instrument, then change to the smaller range once you know the current is safe.

A **galvanometer** measures smaller currents.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electric circuit** | A continuous conducting path connected between the terminals of a battery |
| **Complete circuit** | A continuous conducting path |
| **Open circuit** | A circuit with a break in it, so no current flows |
| **Short circuit** | A circuit in which two wires that should not have touched have touched |
| **Ground** | A common conductor to which wires are connected to provide continuity |
| **Electric current** | The net amount of charge that passes through the wire's full cross-section at any point per unit time, $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$ |
| **Ampere (A)** | The unit of current; $1\ \mathrm{A} = 1\ \mathrm{C/s}$ |
| **Conventional current** | The direction positive charge would flow, from high potential to low potential |
| **Electron current** | The direction of electron flow, from low potential to high potential |
| **Conservation of electric charge** | Charge does not disappear; a steady current is the same at every point of a circuit at any instant |
| **Ammeter** | A device that measures electric current, connected in series, with $R \approx 0$ |
| **Galvanometer** | A device that measures smaller currents |

# 18.3 Ohm's Law: Resistance and Resistors

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Potential difference and the energy it carries

The higher the voltage, the more energy there is to push electrons out, and so the greater the flow of current. The energy carried by a charge moved through a potential difference is

$$E = QV$$

where $E$ is energy in joules (J), $Q$ is charge in coulombs (C) and $V$ is the potential difference in volts (V).

A **voltmeter** measures potential difference. Because a potential difference is a difference *across* something, the voltmeter is connected **in parallel** with the component whose voltage is wanted. Its measurement ranges are $0$–$15\ \mathrm{V}$ and $0$–$3\ \mathrm{V}$.

## Ohm's law

**Georg Simon Ohm** established that the current in a metal wire is directly proportional to the potential difference applied to its two ends:

$$I \propto V$$

Written with the constant of proportionality made explicit, this is **Ohm's law**:

$$V = IR$$

with $V$ the voltage in volts (V), $I$ the current in amperes (A) and $R$ the electrical resistance in ohms ($\Omega$).

**Electrical resistance** is the ratio of the potential difference across a resistor to the current through it.

## Resistors

**Resistors** are used to control the amount of current. Their values range from under $1\ \Omega$ to over $10^{6}\ \Omega$. The two main types are:

- **Wire-wound** resistors, which consist of a coil of fine wire.
- **Composition** resistors, usually made of carbon, and thin carbon or metal films.

## Ohmic and non-ohmic materials

Ohm's law is not a fundamental law. It is a description of a certain class of materials — metal conductors. Its precondition is that $R$ is a constant independent of $V$. Materials whose $R$ is not constant are said to be **non-ohmic**; semiconductor diodes and filament lamps are the examples the guide gives.

This has a direct consequence for graphs. On an $I$–$V$ graph the slope is $\dfrac{1}{R}$, so the shape of the curve reads off how the resistance behaves:

| Component | How $R$ behaves | Shape of the $I$–$V$ graph |
|---|---|---|
| Conductor (metal) | $R$ is constant | Straight line — a linear relationship |
| Semiconductor diode | $R$ decreases as $V$ increases | Concave up |
| Filament lamp | $R$ increases as $V$ increases | Concave down |

A rising slope means a falling $R$, and a falling slope means a rising $R$ — which is why the diode's curve bends upwards and the lamp's bends downwards.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Voltmeter** | A device that measures potential differences, connected in parallel |
| **Ohm's law** | $V = IR$: the current in a metal wire is directly proportional to the potential difference applied to its two ends |
| **Electrical resistance** | The ratio of the potential difference across a resistor to the current through it, measured in ohms ($\Omega$) |
| **Resistor** | A component used to control the amount of current; wire-wound (a coil of fine wire) or composition (carbon, or thin carbon or metal films) |
| **Non-ohmic** | Describes a material whose resistance is not constant and independent of $V$, e.g. semiconductor diodes and filament lamps |

# 18.4 Resistivity

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The law of resistance

The resistance $R$ of any wire is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area:

$$R = \rho\frac{L}{A}$$

- $R$: resistance ($\Omega$)
- $\rho$: resistivity ($\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$)
- $L$: length (m)
- $A$: cross-sectional area ($\mathrm{m^2}$)

**Resistivity** is the constant of proportionality in that relationship. Unlike $R$ itself it does not describe a particular piece of wire but the material the wire is made of. It also depends somewhat on purity, heat treatment, temperature and other factors.

## Choosing a material for wires

Resistivity alone does not decide which metal gets used:

| Metal | Property | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Silver | Lowest resistivity, but very expensive | Not used for ordinary wiring |
| Copper | Resistivity close to silver's, and much less expensive | Most wires |
| Aluminium | Higher resistivity, but less dense | Preferable for transmission lines |

Aluminium is the case worth noticing: resistivity is not the only criterion, and here the lower density is what decides.

## Temperature dependence

**For metal conductors, resistance increases with temperature.** As $T$ rises the atoms move more rapidly and are arranged in a less orderly fashion, so they interfere more with the flow of electrons and make them harder to move past.

Provided the temperature change is not too great, resistivity increases nearly linearly with temperature:

$$\rho_T = \rho_0\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)\right]$$

- $\rho_T$: resistivity at temperature $T$ ($\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$)
- $\rho_0$: resistivity at the reference temperature $T_0$, usually taken as $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$
- $\alpha$: temperature coefficient ($1/^\circ\mathrm{C}$)

Because $R = \rho L/A$, multiplying both sides by $L/A$ turns the same statement into one about resistance:

$$R_T = R_0\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)\right]$$

**For semiconductors the effect runs the other way**: resistance and resistivity *decrease* as temperature increases. As $T$ rises, some electrons that were normally not free become free and can contribute to the current flow. The temperature coefficient for a semiconductor can therefore be negative.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Law of resistance** | The resistance of any wire is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, $R = \rho L/A$ |
| **Resistivity ($\rho$)** | The constant of proportionality in $R = \rho L/A$; depends on the material used, and somewhat on purity, heat treatment and temperature ($\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}$) |
| **Temperature coefficient ($\alpha$)** | The constant in $\rho_T = \rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]$, in $1/^\circ\mathrm{C}$; can be negative for semiconductors |

# 18.5 Electric Power

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Where the energy goes

Electrical devices convert electrical energy into other forms — mechanical, thermal and so on. In an ordinary lightbulb only a few percent of the energy is transformed into visible light; the remaining more than 90 per cent becomes thermal energy.

The chain of events inside the filament explains why:

1. Many collisions occur between the moving electrons and the atoms of the wire.
2. In each collision part of the electron's kinetic energy is transferred to the atom.
3. The kinetic energy of the atoms increases, and hence the temperature of the wire increases.
4. This increased thermal energy can then be transferred as heat by conduction, convection or radiation, or as light.

## Power

**Power** is the rate at which energy is transformed. Starting from $E = QV$ and $I = \Delta Q/\Delta t$:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} = \frac{QV}{t} = IV$$

Substituting Ohm's law gives the two other forms, which matter because in practice you rarely know all three of $I$, $V$ and $R$ at once:

$$P = IV = I(IR) = I^2R \qquad\qquad P = IV = \left(\frac{V}{R}\right)V = \frac{V^2}{R}$$

The unit is the **watt (W)**:

$$1\ \mathrm{W} = 1\ \mathrm{J/s} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{kW} = 1000\ \mathrm{W} \qquad 1\ \mathrm{hp} = 746\ \mathrm{W}$$

## Ratings and actual power

Three related terms must be kept apart:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Voltage rating** | The designed voltage of the device |
| **Power rating** | The power when the device is supplied with its designed voltage |
| **Power dissipated** | The actual power the device is using |

It is the power dissipated, not the power rating, that determines how a bulb behaves: the greater the actual power used by a lightbulb, the brighter it is.

## Energy

$$E = Pt$$

with $E$ in joules. Electricity is billed in kilowatt-hours rather than joules:

$$1\ \mathrm{kWh} = (1000\ \mathrm{W})(3600\ \mathrm{s}) = 3.6\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J}$$

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Power** | The rate of energy transformed, $P = E/t = IV = I^2R = V^2/R$ |
| **Watt (W)** | The unit of power; $1\ \mathrm{W} = 1\ \mathrm{J/s}$ |
| **Voltage rating** | The designed voltage of a device |
| **Power rating** | The power of a device when supplied with its designed voltage |
| **Power dissipated** | The actual power used by a device |

# 18.6 Power in Household Circuits

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Overloading, and the two devices that guard against it

A wire is **overloaded** when it carries more current than is safe. Two devices break the circuit before that happens.

A **fuse** is a length of wire designed to melt, and so break the circuit, when the current passing through it goes above a certain level. It is simple and cheap, and its material should have a low melting point and high conductivity. The thicker the fuse wire, the greater the current required to make it melt. Its **rating current** is the labelled maximum effective current it is designed to allow: when

$$I_{\text{effective}} > I_{\text{rating}}$$

the fuse melts and burns. Once a fuse has burnt out it cannot be used again.

A **circuit breaker** is a safety device that uses an electromagnet or a bimetallic strip to shut off the circuit when the current goes above a certain value. Circuit breakers act more quickly than fuses, and can be reset using the outside switch instead of being replaced.

| Type | How it operates |
|---|---|
| **Bimetallic strip circuit breaker** | Heating of the strip causes it to bend so far to one side that the notch in the spring-loaded metal strip drops down over the end |
| **Electromagnet circuit breaker** | Too much current causes the electromagnet to produce a magnetic field strong enough to open the switch |

If a circuit repeatedly burns out a fuse or opens a circuit breaker, there are two possibilities: too many devices are drawing current in that circuit, or there is a short circuit, in which the resistance is very small and so the current is very large.

## Why household circuits are wired in parallel

Household circuits are parallel circuits. There are several paths for the current to take, and the voltage across each component is the same.

- **Advantages.** If one light goes out, the others burn brightly without change. As lights are added, the current flowing through each light does not change.
- **Disadvantage.** Parallel circuits are more difficult to design and build.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Overloaded** | Describes a wire carrying more current than is safe |
| **Fuse** | A length of wire designed to melt, and so break a circuit, when the current through it goes above a certain level |
| **Rating current** | The labelled maximum effective current a fuse is designed to allow |
| **Circuit breaker** | A safety device using an electromagnet or bimetallic strip to shut off the circuit when the current goes above a certain value |

# 18.7 Alternating Current

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Two kinds of current

**Direct current (dc)** moves steadily in one direction. Thomas Alva Edison championed and commercialised it, and a battery is the everyday example.

**Alternating current (ac)** reverses direction many times per second and is commonly sinusoidal. Nikola Tesla developed and championed it, and electric generators are the everyday example. The guide prints that dc was "first found by" Edison and ac "first found by" Tesla; that is an error — neither man discovered a kind of current, and each promoted one side of the late-nineteenth-century dispute over how electricity should be distributed.

## Voltage and current in an ac circuit

The voltage of an ac supply is

$$V = V_0\sin 2\pi f t = V_0\sin\omega t$$

- $V$: the potential, which oscillates between $+V_0$ and $-V_0$ (V)
- $V_0$: peak voltage (V)
- $f$: frequency — the number of complete oscillations made per second ($1/\mathrm{s}$)
- $\omega$: angular frequency, $\omega = 2\pi f$ ($\mathrm{rad/s}$)

Applying Ohm's law to that voltage gives the current:

$$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{V_0}{R}\sin\omega t = I_0\sin\omega t$$

where $I_0$ is the peak current (A). The current is counted positive when electrons flow in one direction and negative when they flow in the opposite direction, so the **average current is zero**.

## Power, and why it is not zero

$$P = I^2R = I_0^2R\sin^2\omega t$$

Although the average current is zero, the average power is not, because the current is squared: $P$ is always positive. This is why an ac supply delivers energy at all, despite the average current cancelling to nothing.

Taking the average of $\sin^2\omega t$ over a cycle gives

$$\bar P = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2R = \tfrac{1}{2}\frac{V_0^2}{R}$$

where $\bar P$ is the average power (W).

## Root-mean-square values

The same factor of $\tfrac12$ appears in the mean square current and voltage:

$$\overline{I^2} = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2 \qquad\qquad \overline{V^2} = \tfrac{1}{2}V_0^2$$

Taking the square root of each defines the **rms (root-mean-square)** values, sometimes called the **effective values**:

$$I_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{I^2}} = \frac{I_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\,I_0 \qquad\qquad V_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{V^2}} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\,V_0$$

Written with these, the average power takes exactly the form the dc power equations had:

$$\bar P = I_{\mathrm{rms}}V_{\mathrm{rms}} \qquad \bar P = \tfrac{1}{2}I_0^2R = I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R \qquad \bar P = \tfrac{1}{2}\frac{V_0^2}{R}$$

That is the point of defining them: a direct current whose values of $I$ and $V$ equal the rms values of $I$ and $V$ for an alternating current will produce the same power.

One consequence of the squaring is worth remembering for graphs: the period of the power is half the period of the voltage and the current.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Direct current (dc)** | Current that moves steadily in one direction |
| **Alternating current (ac)** | Current that reverses direction many times per second, commonly sinusoidal |
| **Peak voltage ($V_0$)** | The maximum value of the oscillating potential, between $+V_0$ and $-V_0$ |
| **Peak current ($I_0$)** | The maximum value of the oscillating current |
| **Frequency ($f$)** | The number of complete oscillations made per second ($1/\mathrm{s}$) |
| **Angular frequency ($\omega$)** | $\omega = 2\pi f$, in $\mathrm{rad/s}$ |
| **Average power ($\bar P$)** | $\bar P = \tfrac12 I_0^2R = I_{\mathrm{rms}}V_{\mathrm{rms}}$ |
| **rms (root-mean-square) values** | $I_{\mathrm{rms}} = I_0/\sqrt2$ and $V_{\mathrm{rms}} = V_0/\sqrt2$; also called the effective values |

# 19.1 EMF and Terminal Voltage

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Electromotive force

**Electromotive force (emf)** is the potential difference between the terminals of a source when no current flows to an external circuit. A source of emf transforms one type of energy — chemical, mechanical, light and so on — into electrical energy. A battery and an electric generator are both sources of emf.

The qualification "when no current flows" is the whole content of this section, because as soon as current *does* flow the terminals no longer read the emf.

## Internal resistance and terminal voltage

**Internal resistance** is the resistance of the battery itself. It is usually small, but it increases as the battery ages.

**Terminal voltage** is the voltage actually measured between the two terminals $a$ and $b$:

$$V_{ab} = V_a - V_b$$

Two cases follow:

| Condition | Terminal voltage |
|---|---|
| No current is drawn from the battery | $V_{ab} = \varepsilon$ |
| A current flows from the battery | $V_{ab} = \varepsilon - Ir$ |

where $V_{ab}$ is the terminal voltage (V), $\varepsilon$ is the emf (V) and $Ir$ is the internal voltage drop (V). The drop $Ir$ is why a battery under load reads lower than the same battery sitting unconnected — the current has to be pushed through the battery's own resistance before it reaches the terminals.

## The circuit equation

Since $V_{ab} = IR$ for the external resistance $R$:

$$IR = \varepsilon - Ir \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \varepsilon = I(R + r)$$

This is a better exemplification of Ohm's law than $V = IR$ alone, because it accounts for every resistance the current meets, inside the source as well as outside it.

The same split applies to power:

$$P_T = P_R + P_r = I^2R + I^2r = I^2(R + r)$$

Some of the energy the source supplies is dissipated inside the source itself, and only $I^2R$ reaches the external circuit.

## Worked example: finding the internal resistance from two voltage readings

*Two resistors are placed in series with a battery of potential $V$. Resistance $R_2$ has the value $1.00\times10^{3}\ \Omega$. A voltmeter shows the potential across $R_1$ to be $3.00\ \mathrm{V}$ and an ammeter shows the current through $R_2$ to be $5.00\ \mathrm{mA}$.*

**Connecting the meters.** The voltmeter goes across $R_1$, in parallel with it, and no existing wire has to be disconnected to do that. The ammeter must carry the current itself, so it goes in series with $R_2$: the wire on one side of $R_2$ is broken and the ammeter inserted into the gap.

**(c) The value of $R_1$.** The resistors are in series, so the ammeter reading is also the current through $R_1$:

$$R_1 = \frac{V_1}{I} = \frac{3.00\ \mathrm{V}}{5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}} = 6.00\times10^{2}\ \Omega$$

**(d) The power dissipated by $R_2$.** Current and resistance are the two quantities known for $R_2$, so use $P = I^2R$:

$$P_2 = I^2R_2 = (5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A})^2(1.00\times10^{3}\ \Omega) = 2.50\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{W}$$

**(e) The terminal voltage $V$ of the battery.** In series the voltages add, and

$$V_2 = IR_2 = (5.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A})(1.00\times10^{3}\ \Omega) = 5.00\ \mathrm{V}$$

$$V_{ab} = V_1 + V_2 = 3.00 + 5.00 = 8.00\ \mathrm{V}$$

**(f) The internal resistance.** With the battery disconnected no current is drawn, so the $8.20\ \mathrm{V}$ measured then is the emf itself. The difference between emf and terminal voltage is the internal drop:

$$\varepsilon - V_{ab} = Ir \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r = \frac{\varepsilon - V_{ab}}{I} = \frac{8.20 - 8.00}{5.00\times10^{-3}} = 40\ \Omega$$

The $0.20\ \mathrm{V}$ that appears to have gone missing between parts (e) and (f) is exactly the voltage lost inside the battery.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Electromotive force (emf, $\varepsilon$)** | The potential difference between the terminals of a source when no current flows to an external circuit |
| **Internal resistance ($r$)** | The resistance of the battery itself; usually small, but it increases as the battery ages |
| **Terminal voltage ($V_{ab}$)** | The actual voltage measured between the two terminals, $V_{ab} = V_a - V_b$; equal to $\varepsilon$ with no current drawn and to $\varepsilon - Ir$ when a current flows |

# 19.2 Resistors in Series and in Parallel

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Series circuits

Two or more resistors are **connected in series** when they are joined end to end along a single path. There is only one path, so if one device is disconnected the current stops in all the others.

**The same current passes through each resistor.**

$$I = I_1 = I_2 = I_3$$

This follows from conservation of charge: any charge that passes through $R_1$ must also pass through the others, so the same $Q$ passes each resistor in the same time and $I$ is the same.

**The total voltage is the sum of the voltages across each resistor**, by conservation of energy:

$$V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$$

Applying Ohm's law to each term:

$$V = IR_1 + IR_2 + IR_3 = I(R_1 + R_2 + R_3) = IR_{eq}$$

$$R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$$

The **equivalent resistance** $R_{eq}$ is a single resistor whose resistance is the same as the total resistance of the circuit — here, the sum of the separate resistors. Since the current is common, the voltages divide in the ratio of the resistances:

$$V_1 : V_2 : V_3 = R_1 : R_2 : R_3$$

Power behaves the same way:

$$P_T = I^2R_T = I^2(R_1 + R_2 + R_3) = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 \qquad P_1 : P_2 : P_3 = R_1 : R_2 : R_3$$

so in a series circuit the **larger resistance gives the brighter lightbulb**.

**Advantage:** simple to design and build. **Disadvantages:** if one light goes out, all the lights go out; and the lightbulbs become dimmer as more bulbs are added.

## Parallel circuits

Resistors are **connected in parallel** when the current from the source splits into separate branches or paths.

**The same voltage is across each resistor:**

$$V = V_1 = V_2 = V_3$$

**The total current is the sum of the currents flowing through each resistor:**

$$I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3$$

Applying Ohm's law, $I = V/R_{eq}$, and

$$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3} \qquad I_1 : I_2 : I_3 = \frac{1}{R_1} : \frac{1}{R_2} : \frac{1}{R_3}$$

Because the voltage is now the common quantity, the ratios invert: the *smallest* resistance takes the largest share of the current.

$$P_T = I_TV = (I_1 + I_2 + I_3)V = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 \qquad P_1 : P_2 : P_3 = \frac{1}{R_1} : \frac{1}{R_2} : \frac{1}{R_3}$$

**Advantages:** if there is a break in one branch, current can still move through the other branches; and the brightness of the original lightbulbs does not change when more are added (ignoring $r$). **Disadvantages:** more difficult to design and build; and adding too many appliances will increase the current too much, which might heat up the wire and cause a fire.

## Worked example: adding a lamp in parallel

*A lamp, a voltmeter $V$, an ammeter $A$ and a battery with zero internal resistance are connected together. A second lamp is then connected in parallel with the first.*

**How does the ammeter's reading change?** *It increases, because the net resistance of the circuit decreases.* Adding a resistance in parallel always lowers $R_{eq}$ — the reciprocals add, so $1/R_{eq}$ grows and $R_{eq}$ shrinks. The ammeter sits where the whole current passes, so with the same voltage across a smaller $R_{eq}$ it reads a larger $I = V/R_{eq}$. The tempting answer, that the current "splits to feed both branches" and so falls, confuses the current in one branch with the current through the ammeter.

**How does the voltmeter's reading change?** *It remains the same, because the voltmeter is connected to the two ends of the battery.* The voltmeter reads the terminal voltage, and with zero internal resistance $V_{ab} = \varepsilon - Ir = \varepsilon$ no matter how much current is drawn. The second branch therefore changes the current without changing the voltage — which is exactly the property that makes parallel wiring usable in houses.

## 19.2(2) Combined circuits

A **combined circuit** is a circuit which includes both series and parallel branches — a parallel-series or a series-parallel arrangement. The guide flags this as one of the two focuses of the final.

The problem-solving strategy is fixed:

1. Figure out the series or parallel relationships between the resistors in the circuit.
2. Get $R_{eq}$.
3. Get $I_{\text{total}}$ and $V_{\text{total}}$.
4. Find the individual $V$, $I$ and $P$.

*Worked example.* A circuit contains a $2\ \Omega$ resistor and two $4.0\ \Omega$ resistors, with a switch that changes how they are connected. Begin by settling the relationships for the switch position in question. With the switch off, the two $4.0\ \Omega$ resistors are in parallel with each other and that combination is in series with the $2\ \Omega$ resistor.

**Step 2.** The parallel pair first:

$$\frac{1}{R_{eq}} = \frac{1}{4.0} + \frac{1}{4.0} = \frac{1}{2.0} \qquad R_{eq} = 2.0\ \Omega$$

then the total, since this pair is in series with the $2\ \Omega$ resistor:

$$R_{\text{total}} = 2\ \Omega + 2.0\ \Omega = 4.0\ \Omega$$

**Step 3.**

$$I_{\text{total}} = \frac{V_{\text{total}}}{R_{\text{total}}}$$

**Step 4.** Work outwards from what each element shares with the rest of the circuit.

- The $2\ \Omega$ resistor is in series with everything else, so it carries the whole current: $I_{2\Omega} = I_{\text{total}}$, and its voltage is its share of the total,

$$V_{2\Omega} = V_{\text{total}}\times\frac{2\ \Omega}{R_{\text{total}}} = \tfrac{1}{2}V_{\text{total}}$$

- The two $4.0\ \Omega$ resistors are in parallel, so their currents *sum* to $I_{\text{total}}$ while their voltages are equal to each other:

$$V_{4.0\Omega} = V_{\text{total}}\times\frac{R_{eq}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \tfrac{1}{2}V_{\text{total}}$$

The two halves add back to $V_{\text{total}}$, which is the check worth doing at the end of any combined-circuit problem.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Connected in series** | Two or more resistors connected end to end along a single path |
| **Connected in parallel** | Resistors arranged so that the current from the source splits into separate branches or paths |
| **Equivalent resistance ($R_{eq}$)** | A single resistor with the resistance that is the same as the total resistance of the circuit |
| **Combined circuit** | A circuit which includes both series and parallel branches |

# 20.1 Magnets and Magnetic Fields

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## History of magnetism

The ancient Greeks and Chinese discovered that lodestone could attract iron objects and other lodestone. Chinese sailors employed magnets as navigation compasses approximately 900 years ago.

## Magnets and magnetic poles

A **magnet** is an object surrounded by a magnetic field which has the property of attracting ferromagnetic materials — iron, nickel and cobalt. A compass needle is simply a bar magnet supported at its centre of gravity so that it can rotate freely.

The **magnetic poles** are the areas of a magnet where the magnetic effect is strongest. Every magnet is **polarised**: it has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S). The N pole is the north-seeking pole and the S pole is the south-seeking pole — the names describe which way the pole turns when the magnet is free to rotate.

Between magnets, **like poles repel and unlike poles attract**.

Magnetic poles always appear in pairs. Monopoles of magnets do not exist.

## Magnetism and magnetic domains

**Ferromagnetism** is the strong magnetic effect shown by iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, and some of their oxides and alloys.

Its source lies inside the atoms and then in how the atoms group together:

- The spinning and orbiting motion of the electrons makes each atom a tiny magnet.
- A cluster of billions of atoms whose magnetic fields are all lined up in the same way forms a **magnetic domain**. Each domain is itself like a tiny magnet.

**Magnetisation** is then a question of how the domains are arranged. An unmagnetised piece of iron is made up of domains that are randomly arranged, so their fields cancel. In a magnet the domains are aligned in one direction, and the magnetisation process may also alter their size.

## Induced magnetism and making a magnet

Both the N and the S pole of a magnet attract metals such as iron and steel. This is because unmagnetised materials such as steel and iron acquire two opposite magnetic poles when placed in the neighbourhood of a magnet — the material becomes a magnet itself, oriented so as to be attracted. That is how **induced magnetism** arises.

Two ways of making a magnet follow:

- Place the unmagnetised material near a magnet. This gains only weak magnetism.
- Use an **electromagnet**: pass a direct current through a coil of wire placed outside the material.

## Hard and soft magnetic materials

Magnetic materials are classified by how well they keep their magnetism.

| | Hard magnetic materials | Soft magnetic materials |
|---|---|---|
| Behaviour | Difficult to magnetise, but do not readily lose their magnetism | Relatively easy to magnetise, but their magnetism is only temporary |
| Used for | Permanent magnets | Temporary magnets — the cores of electromagnets and transformers, because their magnetic effect can be switched on or off or reversed easily |
| Examples | Steel, and the alloys Alnico, Alcomax and Magnadur | Iron (soft iron) and Mumetal |

**Non-magnetic materials** include the metals brass, copper, zinc, tin and aluminium, as well as non-metals.

## Demagnetising a magnet

Both methods work by destroying the alignment of the domains:

- Drop a magnet on the floor or strike it with a hammer. The principle is to jar the domains into randomness, and the magnet loses some or all of its magnetism.
- Heat a permanent magnet. Raising the temperature increases the random thermal motion of the atoms, which tends to randomise the domains. Above a certain temperature the material loses the property of ferromagnetism altogether.

## The magnetic field and its field lines

The **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where the magnetic force is exerted.

It can be investigated in two ways. A small compass can be used: the direction of the magnetic field $B$ at any point is the same as the direction the compass indicates. Alternatively the field can be mapped out with iron filings, which line up along it. In both cases the field $B$ is strong where the lines are dense and weak where they are sparse.

**Magnetic field lines** are imaginary lines used to map out the magnetic field around a magnet. They are three-dimensional. The field direction is defined as the direction in which the force on an N pole would act. This definition fixes the arrows:

- Outside the magnet, the lines run from N to S.
- Inside the magnet, they run from S to N.
- A compass placed at any point lies tangent to the line of force passing through that point.
- The density of the lines represents how strong the magnetic field is.

Where two magnets sit near one another their fields superpose into a single combined field.

Bringing other materials into a field has different effects depending on the material. Glass produces no reaction. In a ferromagnetic material the field lines become concentrated within the material, and the material is magnetised by induction: the end closest to the N pole of the magnet becomes the S pole of the material, and the end closest to the S pole of the magnet becomes the N pole.

Between two wide poles of a magnet the magnetic field is nearly **uniform**, except near the edges.

## Earth as a magnet

Earth's magnetism is due to the circulation of the molten metal within Earth's core. The Earth is a large weak magnet with its magnetic S pole — the south-seeking pole — under a point in Canada.

Two angles describe how a compass behaves at a given place:

- **Magnetic declination** is the angular difference between the direction of a compass needle, which points along the magnetic field lines, and true (geographical) north at that location.
- **The angle of dip**, or angle of inclination, is the angle that the Earth's magnetic field makes with the horizontal at any point. It is not zero because the Earth's magnetic field at most locations is not tangent to the Earth's surface.

The field is not fixed. Magnetic poles reverse themselves periodically, and Earth's north magnetic pole has been moving over time, on the order of 10 km per year in recent decades. Magnetism in rocks solidified at various times in the past — their ages determined by radioactive dating — suggests that the poles reversed direction 400 times over the last 330 million years.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Magnet** | An object surrounded by a magnetic field which has the property of attracting ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) |
| **Magnetic poles** | The areas of a magnet where the magnetic effect is strongest |
| **Ferromagnetism** | The strong magnetic effect shown by iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium, and some of their oxides and alloys |
| **Magnetic domain** | A cluster of billions of atoms whose magnetic fields are all lined up in the same way; each domain is like a tiny magnet |
| **Magnetisation** | The process by which randomly arranged domains become aligned in one direction, their size possibly being altered too |
| **Induced magnetism** | The magnetism acquired by an unmagnetised material such as iron or steel, which gains two opposite poles when placed near a magnet |
| **Electromagnet** | A magnet made by passing direct current through a coil of wire placed outside the material |
| **Hard magnetic materials** | Materials difficult to magnetise that do not readily lose their magnetism; used for permanent magnets |
| **Soft magnetic materials** | Materials relatively easy to magnetise whose magnetism is only temporary; used for temporary magnets and the cores of electromagnets and transformers |
| **Magnetic field** | The region around a magnet where the magnetic force is exerted |
| **Magnetic field lines** | Imaginary three-dimensional lines mapping out the magnetic field, directed as the force on an N pole would act |
| **Magnetic declination** | The angular difference between the direction of a compass needle at any location and true (geographical) north |
| **Angle of dip (angle of inclination)** | The angle that the Earth's magnetic field makes with the horizontal at any point |

# 20.2 Electric Currents Produce Magnetic Fields

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Oersted's experiment

Hans Christian Oersted (1777–1851) made the discovery in 1820 that magnetism and electricity are related.

- The compass needle deflects if, and only if, the wire carries an electric current.
- Whenever he turned on the electricity, the compass needles lined up in a circle around the wire.
- Iron filings also align along the direction of the magnetic field lines near a straight current-carrying wire.

The "if and only if" is the important half: a wire with no current does nothing, so it is the current, not the metal, that produces the field.

## The magnetic field around a wire

If an electric current is passed through a wire, a weak magnetic field is produced. It has three features:

- The magnetic field lines are circles.
- The field is strongest close to the wire.
- Increasing the current increases the strength of the field.

The direction of the current $I$ determines the direction of the magnetic field $B$. Use the **1st right-hand rule**: grip the wire with the right hand so that the thumb points along the conventional current, and the fingers curl in the direction of the field lines.

*Worked example.* A long straight wire conductor carries a constant, stable conventional current towards the north. A compass is placed directly above the wire. When a large conventional current flows, which way does the N pole of the compass point?

Point the right thumb north along the current. The fingers curl over the top of the wire towards the east, so at a point directly above the wire the field runs east. A compass needle lies along the field, so its **N pole points east**.

## Magnetic field due to a long straight wire (section 20.5)

$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$

where $\mu_0$ is the **permeability of free space**,

$$\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\cdot m/A}$$

and $r$ is the distance from the wire. The standard unit of magnetic field $B$ is the **tesla (T)**. The $1/r$ in the formula is the quantitative form of "the field is strongest close to the wire", and the $I$ on top is "increasing the current increases the field".

## Combining the fields of two wires

When two wires are present, both the magnitude and the direction of $B$ must be found for each wire separately and then combined. Two cases recur.

**Where do the fields cancel?** *Two very long current-carrying wires are shown end on. The wire on the left carries $4\ \mathrm{A}$ into the plane of the paper and the wire on the right carries $3\ \mathrm{A}$ out of the paper. Disregarding $x\to\infty$, in which region of the $x$-axis could the two fields add to zero?*

Because the currents are in opposite directions, the two fields point the *same* way in the region between the wires, so they can never cancel there. Outside the pair they oppose, and cancellation requires

$$\frac{\mu_0(4\ \mathrm{A})}{2\pi d_1} = \frac{\mu_0(3\ \mathrm{A})}{2\pi d_2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{d_1}{d_2} = \frac{4}{3}$$

so the point must be further from the $4\ \mathrm{A}$ wire than from the $3\ \mathrm{A}$ wire. That is only possible on the far side of the weaker wire — the region beyond the $3\ \mathrm{A}$ wire, region III, and no other.

**What is the resultant at a given point?** *A long pair of insulated wires conducts $24.5\ \mathrm{A}$ of dc current to and from an instrument. The wires are of negligible diameter and are $2.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. What is the magnetic field $10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from their midpoint, in their plane? Compare it with the magnetic field of the Earth.*

"To and from" means the two currents are equal and opposite. Each wire lies $1.4\ \mathrm{mm}$ from the midpoint, so the field point is at

$$r_1 = 0.100 - 0.0014 = 0.0986\ \mathrm{m} \qquad r_2 = 0.100 + 0.0014 = 0.1014\ \mathrm{m}$$

At a point in the plane of the wires and outside the pair, the two fields are antiparallel, so they subtract:

$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}\left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right) = (2\times10^{-7})(24.5)\left(\frac{1}{0.0986} - \frac{1}{0.1014}\right)$$

$$B = (4.9\times10^{-6})(10.142 - 9.862) = 1.4\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{T}$$

The nearer wire wins, so the resultant takes its direction, which in the figure is into the page. Comparing with the Earth's field of $5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$:

$$\frac{1.4\times10^{-6}}{5\times10^{-5}} \approx 0.03$$

so $B$ is about **3 per cent of $B_E$**. Notice how much the near-cancellation costs: each wire on its own would give about $5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$ at this point, and together they give a field more than thirty times smaller. Two nearly cancelling fields is what makes this pair of leads worth comparing with the Earth's field at all.

## Magnetic field for coils (section 20.7, solenoids)

A **solenoid** is a current-carrying coil of wire with many loops.

- The magnetic field lines are bunched up inside the loop.
- Increasing the number of loops increases the field.

A solenoid acts like a magnet: one end can be considered the north pole and the other the south pole. Increasing the current increases the strength of the field. Unlike a bar magnet, the field is temporary — it is turned on and off by switching the current on and off — and the north and south poles change with the direction of the current.

To find the poles of the solenoid, use the **2nd right-hand rule**, which also works in reverse to find the direction of the current in the wires:

- Grip the coil with your right hand.
- Your fingers point in the conventional current direction.
- Your thumb points towards the N pole of the coil.

Two consequences worth stating as true-or-false drill: the right-hand rule *can* be used to determine the direction of the magnetic field inside a solenoid when the current direction is known, since the rule relates current direction to field in exactly that way. But the claim that the field strength inside a solenoid *increases* if the number of turns per unit length decreases is false — more loops means a stronger field, so fewer turns per unit length gives a weaker one.

## Electromagnets

If a piece of iron is placed inside a solenoid, the magnetic field is increased greatly, because the iron itself becomes a magnet. The resulting magnetic field is the sum of the field due to the current and the field due to the iron, and can be hundreds or thousands of times the field due to the current alone.

The properties of electromagnets are basically those of solenoids, with the iron core added as a fourth:

- Can be switched on and off freely.
- $I$ increases, $B$ increases.
- Number of loops increases, $B$ increases.
- Soft iron core added, $B$ increases.

Applications include the electromagnetic crane, magnetic circuit breakers, the doorbell, and the magnetisation and demagnetisation of magnets:

- **To magnetise** a magnet, insert the material into the solenoid.
- **To demagnetise** a magnet, slowly pull it out of a solenoid through which an alternating current is passing. The ac produces a magnetic field which changes direction very rapidly and throws the atoms in the magnet out of line.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **1st right-hand rule** | The rule giving the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire from the direction of the conventional current |
| **Permeability of free space ($\mu_0$)** | The constant $4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\cdot m/A}$ appearing in $B = \mu_0 I/2\pi r$ |
| **Tesla (T)** | The standard unit of magnetic field $B$ |
| **Solenoid** | A current-carrying coil of wire with many loops |
| **2nd right-hand rule** | Grip the coil with the right hand, fingers in the conventional current direction; the thumb points towards the N pole of the coil |
| **Electromagnet** | A solenoid with a piece of iron placed inside it, whose field is the sum of the field due to the current and the field due to the iron |

# 20.3 Force on an Electric Current in a Magnetic Field

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Ampère's force

Section 20.2 showed that a current produces a magnetic field. The converse also holds: a magnet exerts a force on a current-carrying wire. This is **Ampère's force**.

$$F = Il_\perp B = IlB\sin\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the current direction and the magnetic field, and $l_\perp$ is the component of the wire's length perpendicular to $B$. The two extremes follow immediately from the sine:

$$F_{\max} = IlB \quad \text{when } \theta = 90^\circ\ (\text{wire} \perp \text{magnetic field})$$

$$F_{\min} = 0 \quad \text{when } \theta = 0^\circ\ (\text{wire} \parallel \text{magnetic field})$$

So the statement that the magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is zero if the wire is parallel to the magnetic field is **true** — $\sin 0^\circ = 0$ removes the force entirely.

The standard unit of $B$, the **tesla (T)**, is derived from this formula:

$$1\ \mathrm{T} = 1\ \mathrm{N/(A\cdot m)}$$

## How big are real magnetic fields?

| Field | Magnitude |
|---|---|
| Earth's magnetic field | $5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T} = 0.5$ gauss |
| Strongest permanent magnets | near $2\ \mathrm{T}$ |
| Superconducting electromagnets | $10\ \mathrm{T}$ or more |

with $1\ \text{gauss} = 1\ \mathrm{G} = 1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{T}$.

## Direction of the force

To find the direction of the force — or, given the force, of the current or the field — use the **3rd right-hand rule (RHR)**.

## Force between two parallel wires (section 20.6)

Each wire produces a magnetic field at the position of the other, and each therefore sits in a field and feels Ampère's force. The result depends only on the relative direction of the two currents:

- **Currents in the same direction — attraction.**
- **Currents in opposite directions — repulsion.**

*Worked example.* Two light conductor wires are hung vertically, with the electrical current in both wires directed upwards. What happens? The currents are in the same direction, so **the wires experience a force of attraction**. The forces do not cancel — they are an action-reaction pair pulling the two wires together, not two forces on one object.

The magnitude, derived from Ampère's law, is a force per unit length:

$$\frac{F}{l} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$

where $d$ is the centre-to-centre separation of the wires. The structure of the expression is the field of one wire, $\mu_0I_1/2\pi d$, multiplied by $I_2l$ from $F = IlB$.

*Worked example.* *A long pair of insulated wires carries $24.5\ \mathrm{A}$ to and from an instrument, the two wires being $2.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. A third wire is placed in the plane of the two, parallel and just to the right, carrying $25.0\ \mathrm{A}$ upward, $2.8\ \mathrm{mm}$ from the nearest wire centre to centre. What force per metre of length does it exert on each of the other two wires?*

Both other wires carry $24.5\ \mathrm{A}$, so only the separations and the current directions differ. The common factor is

$$\frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi} = (2\times10^{-7})(25.0)(24.5) = 1.225\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N}$$

**The nearer wire**, at $d = 2.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$:

$$\frac{F}{l} = \frac{1.225\times10^{-4}}{2.8\times10^{-3}} = 4.4\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N/m}$$

Its current runs the same way as the third wire's, so this force is **attractive**.

**The further wire**, at $d = 2.8 + 2.8 = 5.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$:

$$\frac{F}{l} = \frac{1.225\times10^{-4}}{5.6\times10^{-3}} = 2.2\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N/m}$$

It carries the return current, in the opposite direction, so this force is **repulsive**. Doubling the separation has halved the force, as the $1/d$ requires, and because one force is attractive and the other repulsive the two partly cancel on the third wire.

## Applications

Applications of the force on a current in a magnetic field include the galvanometer, the motor and the loudspeaker.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Ampère's force** | The force a magnet exerts on a current-carrying wire, $F = Il_\perp B = IlB\sin\theta$ |
| **Tesla (T)** | The standard unit of magnetic field, $1\ \mathrm{T} = 1\ \mathrm{N/(A\cdot m)}$ |
| **Gauss (G)** | A smaller unit of magnetic field, $1\ \mathrm{G} = 1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{T}$ |
| **3rd right-hand rule** | The rule giving the direction of the force on a current in a magnetic field, or of the current or field given the other two |

# 20.4 Force on an Electric Charge Moving in a Magnetic Field

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The guide covers Part A of this section only.

## The Lorentz force

The **Lorentz force** is the force that free moving charged particles experience when they pass through a magnetic field. Its magnitude is

$$F = qvB\sin\theta$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the directions of $v$ and $B$.

This is not a new law but the same Ampère force written for one particle. If $N$ particles of charge $q$ pass a given point in time $t$, they constitute a current

$$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{Nq}{t}, \qquad \frac{l}{t} = v$$

so that

$$F = IlB\sin\theta = \frac{Nq\,l\,B\sin\theta}{t} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F = qvB\sin\theta$$

The extremes follow from the sine, exactly as in 20.3:

$$F_{\max} = qvB \quad \text{when } \theta = 90^\circ\ (\text{charge moves} \perp \text{magnetic field})$$

$$F_{\min} = 0 \quad \text{when } \theta = 0^\circ\ (\text{charge moves} \parallel \text{magnetic field})$$

(The guide labels the $\theta = 0^\circ$ line $F_{\max}$; it is the minimum, as the same guide's 20.3 states for the parallel case.)

The direction of the force is given by the **3rd right-hand rule**, almost the same rule used to find the direction of the Ampère force.

Two immediate consequences are worth stating outright. A charged particle entering a uniform field *parallel* to its velocity **experiences no change in velocity**, since $\sin 0^\circ = 0$ and there is no force at all. And a charged particle **at rest** in a uniform magnetic field experiences **no** magnetic force, because $v = 0$ makes $F = qvB\sin\theta$ vanish however strong the field.

## Worked example: the force on a proton approaching a current-carrying wire

*The conventional current $I$ in a long straight wire flows upward. At the instant a proton of charge $+e$ is a distance $R$ from the wire and heading directly towards it, what is the force on the proton?*

Two steps: get $B$ at the proton, then apply the Lorentz force.

The wire's field at distance $R$ has magnitude $B = \mu_0 I/2\pi R$, and the 1st right-hand rule puts it into the page on one side of the wire and out of the page on the other. Applying the 3rd right-hand rule with $v$ pointing at the wire gives a force **downward — opposite to the direction of $I$**. The answer is the same whichever side of the wire the proton is on, because moving to the other side reverses both $v$ and $B$, and reversing both leaves the force unchanged.

The magnitude combines the two formulas:

$$F = evB = ev\cdot\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} = \frac{\mu_0 evI}{2\pi R}$$

## Worked example: crossed fields

*A positively charged particle moves to the right into a region where an electric field is directed up the plane of the paper. In which direction must the magnetic field point so that the particle maintains a constant velocity?*

Constant velocity means zero net force. The electric field pushes the positive charge up the page, so the magnetic force must be equal in size and directed down the page. With $v$ to the right, the 3rd right-hand rule gives a downward force on a positive charge when the magnetic field points **out of the plane of the page**.

## The circular path

If a charged particle is moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, its path will be a **circle**. The reason is that the force is always perpendicular to the motion: it changes the direction of $v$ without ever changing its magnitude, which is precisely the condition for uniform circular motion.

Setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force,

$$F_{\text{net}} = F_C = F_B \qquad \frac{mv^2}{r} = qvB \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad r = \frac{mv}{qB} \qquad r \propto v$$

The period follows:

$$T = \frac{2\pi r}{v} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$$

and the striking feature is that **$T$ is not related to $v$**: the $v$ in the numerator of $2\pi r$ cancels the $v$ hidden in $r$. A fast particle travels a proportionately larger circle in the same time.

The reciprocal of the period is the **cyclotron frequency**, the frequency at which particles revolve in a cyclotron:

$$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}$$

## Charge separation in a moving wire

A wire moved through a magnetic field experiences an induced charge separation. The mechanism is the Lorentz force again: the free charges inside the wire are carried along at the wire's velocity, so each of them feels $F = qvB\sin\theta$, and that force drives them along the wire towards one end. One end becomes positive and the other negative.

The 3rd right-hand rule, applied to the wire's velocity and the field, gives the direction the positive charge is pushed — so given any two of the velocity, the field and the observed separation of charge, the third can be deduced.

## The aurora

Charged ions approach the Earth from the Sun — the "solar wind" — and enter the atmosphere mainly near the poles, ionising the air; as the electrons recombine with the atoms, light is emitted.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Lorentz force** | The force that free moving charged particles experience when they pass through a magnetic field, $F = qvB\sin\theta$ |
| **Cyclotron frequency** | The frequency at which particles revolve in a cyclotron, $f = 1/T = qB/2\pi m$ |
| **Aurora** | Light emitted when charged ions from the solar wind enter the atmosphere near the poles, ionise the air, and the electrons then recombine with atoms |
